item.title: Why Password Spreadsheets Fail to Capture Employee Credential Behavior
item.description:
Why Password Spreadsheets Fail to Capture Employee Credential Behavior

Password spreadsheets used by administrators often present a false sense of completeness, as they only reflect credentials that employees have explicitly reported, missing passwords that have been changed, created, or shared since the last update.

🔍 The Visibility Gap

Administrators may believe they have a handle on company credentials, but this view is incomplete unless someone actively updates the document. Work passwords frequently end up in untracked locations, including:

  • Browser built-in storage
  • Shared Google documents or chat messages (e.g., Slack)
  • Personal vaults used because official access is too slow
  • Sticky notes on desks

⚙️ Drivers of Unreported Use

The predominant factor in this behavior is convenience. When approved processes are slow or unclear, employees prioritize getting work done by using tools immediately at hand, even if they know it violates rules. Because employees rarely manually report every new password, update, or shared credential, these spreadsheets fail to capture the actual state of credential usage.

📊 Credential Weakness and Reuse

Lack of visibility prevents companies from knowing if critical assets are protected by weak passwords. Evidence highlights significant risks:

  • Reuse: Verizon’s 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report found that in the median case, only 49% of users’ passwords were unique, meaning more than half were reused across services.
  • Weakness: The ‘TOP 20 Not-So-Secret Business Passwords’ report by NordPass identified ‘123456’ as the most common corporate password.
  • Complexity: Verizon’s report found that only 3% of compromised passwords in its dataset met basic complexity standards.

Without visibility into storage locations, admins cannot determine who uses a password, who it has been shared with, or if it has been changed. Consequently, they cannot assess the strength or reuse of daily credentials.

⚠️ Security Implications

If attackers gain access to a password spreadsheet, they may encrypt it for ransom or use the credentials inside to access other systems, spreading the attack further. The 2026 edition of the Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report identified credential abuse as the initial access vector in 13% of breaches, while vulnerability exploitation accounted for 31%, underscoring the need for integrated credential protection.

To keep accounts protected, admins need to answer specific questions about each password: Is it strong? Who owns it? Where is it stored? Who has access? Is it reused, old, or exposed in a breach? Strong passwords are still at risk if reused across accounts, as exposure in one breach can lead to access to others.

💡 Mitigation Features

Tools like NordPass allow administrators to set password requirements to ensure strength and enable users to share credentials over protected channels. Key features include:

  • Sharing Hub: Displays who has access to passwords shared with multiple people or teams.
  • Activity Log: Records actions related to company passwords.

#PasswordManagement #Cybersecurity #CredentialSecurity #DataBreach

Source: Still tracking company passwords in spreadsheets? You’re flying blind.

item.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Integrates with Okta Cross App Access for Secure Agent Governance
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Integrates with Okta Cross App Access for Secure Agent Governance

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale using any framework or model. A new integration with Okta Cross App Access (XAA) allows organizations to manage agent identity and governance directly within their identity provider (IdP).

🔍 Overview

This solution establishes a clear separation between governance and execution. Okta serves as the governance plane, deciding which agent may act for which user against specific resources. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore serves as the execution plane, managing credentials and turning governance decisions into valid access tokens.

Component Role
Okta Governance plane: decides which agent acts for which user against which resource.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity Execution plane: holds credentials and redeems grants for tokens in a vault.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime Validates Okta’s grant.

🧩 How it works

The identity flow ensures that agent actions are always tied to a verified user session:

  • User Sign-in: Users access a backend for frontend (BFF) using OpenID Connect via the agent’s linked Okta app.
  • Token Exchange: For each request, the BFF performs an RFC 8693 token exchange, trading the user’s ID token for an Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG) at Okta’s authorization server.
  • Okta Verification: Okta checks that the agent is active, the user is assigned to it, and an administrator has approved the applications and scopes the agent might reach.
  • Execution: The BFF invokes the agent on the AgentCore runtime using the ID-JAG. AgentCore Identity then redeems the ID-JAG for a short-lived access token accepted by the resource.

⚙️ Key details

The system utilizes three distinct tokens to record different decisions throughout the request lifecycle:

  • ID Token: Identifies the user.
  • Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG): Represents Okta’s decision; single-use and expires in 5 minutes.
  • Access Token: Issued by Okta’s custom authorization server, naming both the user and the agent.

In testing, the governance process proved highly responsive. When an administrator removed a user’s assignment, Okta refused new agent requests for that user within approximately 1 second. Existing tokens expired within 5 minutes. Performance testing showed that AgentCore Identity added roughly 0.6 seconds of latency to a request taking 30 seconds end to end.

🚀 Availability

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore charges based on usage. A technical walkthrough for building a task agent with this governance model takes about 1 hour. The associated sample code is provided for non-production use, and organizations should consult with security and legal teams before deployment.

#AWS #AmazonBedrock #Okta #AIagents #Cybersecurity

Source: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 1 | Amazon Web Services
